newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - refiners play wait-and-see.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - refiners play wait-and-see.

text.p: U.S. crude prices are expected to stay weaker through to at least Wednesday as the expiry of the December contract on the NYMEX keeps cash market participants out of the market, traders said.
Cash traders said the relative quiet seen in the markets was also partially based on refiners waiting to see if December outright prices slip into contango against the January.
"The expiration on Wednesday always clouds the issue, but the refiners are looking for contango in the Dec/Jan before it comes off the board," said a Texas cash crude trader.
Monday morning saw the spread between the Dec/Jan NYMEX at 19-21 cts, with December West Texas Intermediate/Cushing hovering around the $24.00 a barrel level.
Expiration fluctuations aside, traders said the weather and its effect on heating oil stocks were keys to watch.
Inventory data in the weekly American Petroleum Institute (API) report for Tuesday should provide that information.
Bill O'Grady, oil analyst for A.G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis, said prices were now tied to what is now the "weather season."
"If the weather gets cold (outright crude and products) prices go up, if it is warm then prices go down. Heating oil will lead the market around by its nose," Edwards said.
Forecasts call for three to five days of warmer temperatures in the key heating oil regions in the U.S. Northeast, but then colder weather is slated from the weekend.
Outside of distillate data, the weather and expiry, traders will eye pre-OPEC reports for possible surprises.

"All of the members (of OPEC) are cheating a little, except Iran. It doesn't really seem to matter, they should leave the quota the same," Edwards said, noting with world oil prices strong, the impetus to change the status quo is faint.
OPEC is scheduled to start official meetings in Vienna on November 27, but informal gatherings will start sooner, likely starting the news cycle from the coming weekend.

On the domestic grade front, cash dealers said the status quo also should hold. "Sours will most likely come in a little to start the week, and Light Louisiana Sweet should stay healthy, maybe come up a little," said a trader.
Friday saw LLS/St. James slip around 5 cents on the weak tone in wet Brent established by a heavier-than-expected North Sea loading program.
Still, traders said the Louisina sweets were at extremely strong levels to start. Midland WTI/Cushing was seen staying rangebound at a 1-6 cts premium to the WTI.

Sour grade differentials have remained weak, flooded by fundamental supply. Deals for West Texas Sour/Midland have stayed more than $1.70 below the WTI marker and Eugene Island was valued around a $1.15 discount.
